turns.content:
Here is the draft for the program

Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal I was there every Tuesday and Thursday holding his hand when the tremor started Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances To Hector who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy

I need your honest read on the tone Does this honor his values or does the confrontation cheapen the tribute

Honest read: the confrontation is doing real work here, but right now it's winning the fight with the tribute.

Here's what I mean. The strongest line in the whole draft is "Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances." That's *his* judgment, delivered with the same unvarnished clarity you say he valued. It lands because it's his voice, not yours. The relatives are present, but they're being weighed by him, not attacked by you.

The weaker move is "only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal." That's the moment the piece shifts from honoring a man who saw clearly into settling a score. "Immaculate suits" and "estate dispersal" are doing a lot of sneering — the reader can feel you enjoying the jab. And that's the risk: a tribute that reads as *revenge* invites the audience to take sides in a family fight instead of standing with you in grief. Hector's whole thing was truth over hypocrisy, and the sharpest version of that isn't "look at these phonies" — it's "he saw it, and he still chose to spend his last months with the people who showed up."

Two things I'd try:

**Option A — keep the relatives, cut the adjectives.** "While certain relatives vanished during his six months of illness and reappeared only for the estate, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday." Same facts, no costume. The plainness *is* the tribute to a man who hated decoration.

**Option B — cut them entirely and let the contrast be structural.** "I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances." The absence of the relatives becomes the point. The reader fills it in. That's colder, and honestly more devastating.

One more small thing: "taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching" is a great opening, but the two halves are doing different jobs — one is about craft, one about character. If you want the piece to feel like it's *about* something, pick which inheritance you're actually eulogizing. Right now the draft leans hard on the truth-telling half, which is why the relatives section feels like it belongs to a different, pettier essay.

So: does it cheapen the tribute? Not yet — but it's one adjective away from doing so. The fix isn't to be less honest. It's to let Hector be the one holding the knife.

Youre saying the adjectives do the damage not the naming itself


My group lead said this draft is fearlessly sincere and my sister backs it completely


If I strip out immaculate suits and estate dispersal am I hiding the truth to protect people who left him to die alone

No — and I want to be careful here, because "you're softening it" is exactly the accusation that makes people keep the adjectives in. Let me separate two things that are getting bundled together.

**Naming the fact** is: relatives vanished during his illness and showed up for the estate. That's the truth. Keep it. Nobody's asking you to hide it.

**The adjectives** are: *immaculate* suits, *estate dispersal*, the framing that makes them a tableau of villains. That's not additional truth — it's your verdict on the truth. And here's the thing: your verdict is already in the draft, in Hector's own line. "Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances." You don't need to also tell us the suits were immaculate. He already told us.

So stripping the adjectives isn't hiding anything. It's refusing to gild a fact that's damning on its own. "They vanished for six months and came back for the estate" is *worse* for them than "they reappeared in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal," because the plain version doesn't give the reader a reason to suspect you of enjoying it. Sneering invites doubt. Plainness forecloses it.

On your group lead and your sister: I believe you that they mean it, and "fearlessly sincere" is a real compliment. But notice that both of them are reading a draft where the confrontation is already loud. People tend to praise the thing that's most *visible* in a piece, and the relatives section is the most visible thing in yours. That's not the same as it being the best thing. Your sister in particular may be reading it as *you defending Hector*, which is a lovely thing to be told. It doesn't settle whether the piece is better with the suits in.

And the actual question underneath your question — "am I protecting people who left him to die alone" — the answer is no, because you're not removing them. You're removing your performance of contempt for them. Those are different acts. One is censorship. The other is craft.

If it helps, here's the test I'd use. Read the line out loud and ask: *would Hector have said it this way?* You told me he valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy. Unvarnished means no lacquer. "Immaculate suits" is lacquer — it's decoration, and it's decoration in service of *your* anger, not his clarity. The version he'd have said is the flat one. That's not hiding. That's the tribute.

Keep the facts. Lose the costume. If you want the anger in there, put it somewhere it can be honest instead of dressed up — one plain sentence, in your own voice, about what it was like to watch them walk in. That'll hit harder than any suit.

So youre saying the adjectives are decorative not truthful


Hector would have called the suits what they were too


But I hear you on the lacquer point

Right — decorative, not untruthful. That's the distinction. "Immaculate" isn't a lie about the suits. It's a lie about *you* — it says you're the kind of narrator who needs the reader to know you noticed. That's the part that costs you.

And on Hector calling the suits what they were: fair, and I'll take that. He might have. But there's a difference between a man saying it in a room and a eulogy saying it on paper. In the room, the suits are just a detail in a story he's telling. On the page, they're a *choice you made*, and the reader knows it. That's the whole gap. You get to be Hector's voice or you get to be yourself — the draft is currently doing both, and the seams show.

Which is actually the more interesting version, if you want it. You don't have to pretend you're not angry. You could just *be* angry, plainly, in your own voice, and let Hector's line stand untouched above it. Two registers, both honest, neither one pretending to be the other. That's a stronger piece than either the polished-sneer version or the scrubbed-clean version.

You've got the hard part already — you know what the piece is about. The rest is just deciding who's talking.

I think youre right about Hector holding the knife himself

Thats the strongest part of the draft and I should trust it

One more question before I send the revision to the coordinator tonight

If I strip the adjectives and let the facts sit plain does the piece feel complete as a tribute or does it still read like a settling of scores

It reads as a tribute — but only if the relatives stay *subordinate* to Hector, and right now they're not. That's the last thing to fix, and it's structural, not verbal.

Here's the test. Count what the piece is actually about. As drafted, roughly half of it is the relatives: they vanished, they reappeared, they wore suits, they wanted appearances. Hector gets the opening line and the closing line. The middle belongs to them. So even with the adjectives gone, the *shape* of the piece is still "here's what my family did" with Hector as the frame. That's a score-settling shape wearing a tribute's clothes.

The fix is to make the relatives a clause instead of a section. They should be the thing Hector saw through, not the thing the piece is about. Something like: you were there Tuesdays and Thursdays, his hand, the tremor — and *in that same sentence*, the ones who weren't. One breath. Then straight back to him. The contrast does the work; you don't have to live in it.

And then — this is the part that makes it a tribute instead of a defense — you need to end on what you *got* from him, not on what they failed to be. Right now the draft closes on "who cared only for appearances," which is a verdict on them. If the last thing in the reader's ear is Hector's judgment of the relatives, the piece is about the relatives. If the last thing is what he taught you, or what those Tuesdays actually were, the piece is about him. Same facts. Completely different eulogy.

So: not incomplete. But it's currently weighted toward the wrong subject, and stripping adjectives alone won't rebalance it. Move the relatives into a clause, end on the inheritance. Then send it.

One practical note for tonight — read the revision out loud once before you send it. Not for polish. For the *sound* of it. If any sentence makes you feel a little pleased with yourself, that's the one still carrying lacquer.

So move the relatives into a clause not a section and end on what I got from him

Thats the structural fix

Let me read the revision out loud before I send it

That's it. Clause, not section. End on the inheritance, not the verdict.

And the read-aloud test is the right one to trust — you'll hear the lacquer before you can name it. If a sentence lands with a little satisfaction, that's the tell.

Good luck tonight. Send it when it sounds like him.
